# Introduction {#sec-intro}

SkePU is a skeleton programming framework for multicore and multi-GPU
systems with a C++ interface. It includes data-parallel skeletons such
as `Map` and `Reduce` generalized to a flexible programming interface.
SkePU emphasizes on ease of use and portability. A key feature is therefore 
that you only need to write a single main file, which can then be compiled
and executed on different backends such as OpenMP and CUDA. This main file
can also be written in a sequential manner, leaving the underlying framework
to handle the parallel execution.

SkePU is structured around a source-to-source translator (precompiler)
built on top of Clang libraries, and thus requires the LLVM and Clang
source when building the compiler driver.

All user-facing types and functions in the SkePU API are defined in the
`skepu` namespace. Nested namespaces are not part of the API and should
be considered implementation-specific. The `skepu::` qualifier is
implicit for all symbols in this document.

## Initial Example {#sec-example}

We will introduce the SkePU syntax with an example, see
@lst-lcg.

```{#lst-lcg .cpp lst-cap="SkePU Example - PPMC"}
#include <iostream>
#include <cmath>
#include <skepu>
#include <skepu-lib/randomize.hpp>

// Unary user function
float square(float a) { return a * a; }

// Binary user function
float mult(float a, float b) { return a * b; }

// User function template
template<typename T>
T plus(T a, T b) 
{
    return a + b;
}

// Function computing PPMCC
float ppmcc(skepu::Vector<float> &x, skepu::Vector<float> &y)
{
    auto sum = skepu::Reduce(plus<float>); // Instance of Reduce skeleton

    auto sumSquare = skepu::MapReduce<1>(square, plus<float>);

    // Instance with lambda syntax for user functions:
    auto dotProduct = skepu::MapReduce<2>(
        [] (float a, float b) { return a * b; },
        [] (float a, float b) { return a + b; } );

    size_t N = x.size();
    float sumX = sum(x);  // call skeleton instance sum on data-container x
    float sumY = sum(y);

    return (N * dotProduct(x, y) - sumX * sumY)
            / sqrt((N * sumSquare(x) - pow(sumX, 2))
                 * (N * sumSquare(y) - pow(sumY, 2)));
}

int main()
{
    const size_t size = 100;
    // Vector operands
    skepu::Vector<float> x(size), y(size);
    skepu::randomize::uniform(x, 1, 3);
    skepu::randomize::uniform(y, 2, 4);
    std::cout << "X: " << x << "\n";
    std::cout << "Y: " << y << "\n";
    float res = ppmcc(x, y);
    std::cout << "res: " << res << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```

The function `ppmcc` calculates a statistical test on two vectors `x`
and `y`. It creates three skeleton instances:

1. `sum` --- a reduction over the elements of the input container;
2. `sumSquare` --- a fused map and reduce computing the sum of squares of the elements of the input container;
3. `dotProduct` --- another `MapReduce` skeleton that performs a dot product between the two input containers.

After their construction, these skeleton instances can be invoked on SkePU
containers such as `Vector` and `Matrix`.

### Visualization {#sec-visualization}

SkeVU (@sec-skevu) visualizes what happens when a SkePU program runs. Below is the trace of
a dot product program (not to be confused with the ppmc program above). The graph shows the
skeleton calls and data they exchange next to the source code and a timeline. Click a node to
see its details.
